docs.title: Provider Storage
docs.text: Provider Storage defines one namespaced Crossplane Storage API for S3 buckets, consumer credentials, access grants, and lifecycle rules. Platform operators configure the storage backends. Users do not need to manage provider-specific identities or policies.

docs.title: Responsibility boundary
docs.text:
Platform operators:

  • install the selected backend package and its dependencies;
  • configure the controller identity and backend settings;
  • control who can select a backend, environment, or CloudFerro project; and
  • monitor the generated provider resources and credentials.

Users and higher-level platform services create Storage resources. Each resource represents one principal and can define owned buckets, requests for other buckets, grants to other principals, credential rollover, and lifecycle rules.

Crossplane creates the backend-specific resources and publishes a normalized consumer Secret in the same namespace as the Storage resource. Provider controller credentials are separate and must never be copied to this consumer Secret.

Prepare cloud IAM before use

Managed cloud backends require controller credentials. Prepare them as described in the cloud IAM guide.

docs.title: Documentation path
docs.text:
1. Compare the supported implementations in Backend differences.
  2. Install the selected backend with the Installation guide.
  3. Create and inspect resources with Usage and concepts.
  4. Configure sharing with the Permission model.
  5. Use the API reference for field details.

For repository development and live validation, use the local test guide.

docs.title: ADR-001: Provision Storage on AWS, OTC, and MinIO
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Provider Storage offers one Storage API for AWS S3, OTC OBS, and MinIO. Each backend uses different bucket, identity, credential, and policy resources. A shared Composition would mix these provider-specific models.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Keep the Storage API independent of the backend. Use one Composition for each backend.

Each Composition must:

  1. create the declared buckets;
  2. create the consumer identity, credentials, and permissions;
  3. grant access only after it verifies the bucket owner and the matching grant;
  4. publish the consumer Secret defined in the Consumer Credential Strategy.

An access request is intent only. Access becomes active only when the verified bucket owner grants the requested access level.

The backend resource mapping is:

Backend Bucket Consumer identity Authorization MinIO Bucket User named Policy resources AWS S3 Bucket IAM User and AccessKey IAM Policy and UserPolicyAttachment OTC wrapped OBS Bucket wrapped IAM UserV3 and CredentialV3 OBS BucketPolicy with user IDs

Provider-kubernetes Object resources wrap resources that cannot be composed or observed directly.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A new backend needs a new Composition and backend-specific tests.
  • S3 compatibility does not prove correct provisioning or authorization.
  • Grant logic must verify bucket ownership and discoverability.

docs.title: Current limits
docs.text: • Provider-kubernetes has broad access to provider resources and Secrets. Platform RBAC is part of the security boundary.

docs.title: ADR-002: Rotate Static Credentials by Generation
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: For backends that issue static access keys, an immediate key replacement can break a consumer that has not reloaded its Secret. Keeping too many old keys increases the security risk.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Use spec.credentialsRollover to define the active credential generations:

  • interval is daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, yearly, or none;
  • maxToKeep is the total number of active generations, including the current generation;
  • the default is interval: none and maxToKeep: 1;
  • maxToKeep must be 1 when interval is none.

A time-based generation uses the current UTC period. The suffix format is:

Interval Suffix format daily -YYYYMMDD weekly -YYYYwWW monthly -YYYYMM quarterly -YYYYqQ yearly -YYYY none No suffix

A Composition must calculate the generation once per reconciliation. It must use that value for all identities, credentials, permissions, and Secrets.

Each desired generation creates backend-specific credentials. The first generation is current. Provider Storage writes it to the stable Secret named spec.principal. Crossplane removes generations that are not in the desired set.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Consumers keep one Secret name. They must reload it before an old generation is removed.
  • An overlap gives consumers time to reload, but it also keeps more keys valid.
  • Rotation occurs during reconciliation after the period changes. It does not occur at an exact time.
  • This decision applies only to static access keys.

docs.title: Current limits
docs.text:
• AWS and OTC calculate time in more than one pipeline step. A reconciliation across a period boundary can create inconsistent resource names.
  • OTC policies do not reliably include all retained identities.

docs.title: ADR-003: Run Portable Lifecycle Cleanup Jobs
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Storage API supports Delete and Notify rules. A rule can select objects by age, UTC cutoff, and prefix. Native lifecycle features differ between backends and do not provide the same behavior.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Run lifecycle rules as Kubernetes CronJobs instead of native bucket lifecycle rules.

For each Storage with lifecycle rules, the Composition creates:

  • one ConfigMap with one rclone script for each rule;
  • one CronJob with one container for each rule.

The rules work as follows:

  • Notify lists matching objects and does not change them;
  • Delete removes matching objects;
  • minAge selects objects by relative age;
  • at is a UTC cutoff, not a one-time schedule;
  • a target selects a bucket or a prefix in that bucket.

The default schedule is 17 2 * * *. Operators can change it in the storage EnvironmentConfig.

Jobs use the current consumer Secret and the backend settings from the EnvironmentConfig. They do not receive a Kubernetes service-account token. concurrencyPolicy: Forbid prevents two scheduled Jobs from running at the same time.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Lifecycle behavior is the same for all backends.
  • Cleanup depends on Kubernetes, network access, rclone, and valid consumer credentials.
  • Containers for rules in the same Job run at the same time. Rules with overlapping targets can conflict.
  • An at rule runs on every later schedule. Notify can report the same object more than once.
  • A consumer profile without a Secret needs a separate workload identity for lifecycle Jobs.

docs.title: Current limits
docs.text:
• The API does not reject rules with overlapping targets.
  • The execution order of rules in one Job is not deterministic.

docs.title: ADR-004: Add an OVHcloud S3 Backend
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Provider Storage needs to create S3 buckets and consumer credentials in an OVHcloud Public Cloud project. The project provides OpenStack users, S3 credentials, regional buckets, and per-user S3 policies. Crossplane needs a controller identity with permission to manage these resources.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
During bootstrap, an administrator creates a dedicated OVHcloud IAM service account for the controller. The bootstrap administrator can read the project and create the service account and its IAM policy. Scope the controller policy to the target Public Cloud project and grant the actions needed to manage project users, their S3 credentials and policies, and regional buckets. The controller does not need permission to create IAM service accounts or IAM policies. Store its credentials in the provider Secret.

Use the OVHcloud Composition to create the buckets and the OpenStack users inside that project. It creates S3 credentials and a policy for each consumer user. A separate project user owns the buckets, so a consumer credential change does not change bucket ownership. The consumer receives the same credential Secret contract as for the other backends.

Use standard regional Object Storage. Keep the project ID, storage region, and S3 endpoint in the backend configuration.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The controller service account is distinct from the OpenStack users it creates. The service account's IAM policy controls what Crossplane can manage in the project; each user's S3 policy controls access to buckets and objects.

Removing a bucket from spec.buckets, or removing its Storage resource, requests bucket deletion. OVHcloud rejects deletion while the bucket contains data. S3 policy changes can take time to affect access, so revocation is not immediate.

docs.title: ADR-005: Add a CloudFerro S3 Backend with Project Boundaries
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
CloudFerro uses OpenStack projects for identity and Ceph for S3-compatible object storage. A Keystone EC2 credential belongs to one user and one project. CloudFerro bucket policies identify another project as arn:aws:iam::<PROJECT_ID>:root.

Users with S3 access in the same project can access that project's containers. Separate credentials can be revoked separately, but they do not isolate buckets between users in one project.

Provider-openstack reads the project scope from its JSON authentication configuration. A ProviderConfig has no separate field that overrides the project in that configuration.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Use the OpenStack project as the CloudFerro team and S3 authorization boundary. Assign separate projects to teams that need isolation.

Before Storage reconciliation, cloudferro/dependencies/iam.sh apply selects existing projects by an anchored project-name pattern. It creates one controller user without a default project, assigns the configured member role in each selected project, and verifies project-scoped Object Storage access. The bootstrap administrator login must be able to list these projects, create the controller user in the domain, and assign the project role. The controller user needs only the configured project role. Project creation, portal activation, wallet configuration, and billing remain outside the script.

apply writes one private local credential file that contains the shared controller identity and an array of selected project IDs. It updates the project array after all project checks pass. The render-secrets action reads only that file and prints one namespaced Secret manifest for each project. Its name is cloudferro-project-<project-id> and its key is config. The JSON value contains the controller credentials and the project ID as tenant_id. A static storage EnvironmentConfig contains only endpoint and region settings. Multi-backend installations can select another name with the storages.pkg.internal/environment annotation or label.

A Storage selects the generic Composition and declares its project ID:

metadata:
  annotations:
    storages.pkg.internal/cloudferro-project-id: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
spec:
  crossplane:
    compositionSelector:
      matchLabels:
        provider: cloudferro

The Composition creates one namespaced OpenStack ProviderConfig per Storage. It refers to the deterministic project Secret. All OpenStack managed resources for that Storage refer to the composed ProviderConfig. ContainerV1 therefore uses the project from the Secret. EC2CredentialV3 also uses the current auth scope; the Composition does not pass projectId or userId.

The Composition creates buckets with ContainerV1 and one EC2 credential for each retained Storage credential generation. It publishes the standard consumer Secret. It does not create OpenStack users or role assignments.

For an active cross-project grant, the Composition resolves one discoverable Storage with the matching principal. It reads that Storage's storages.pkg.internal/cloudferro-project-id annotation and creates an AWS S3 BucketPolicy with the grantee project's root ARN. It does not use a peer ProviderConfig lookup. Pending requests and None grants do not add access.

The project annotation is an authorization selector. Admission controls must limit which users and namespaces can set each project ID. Secret read access must be limited to provider workloads and trusted operators.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every S3 user in one project can access that project's buckets. EC2 key rotation and revocation do not provide user-level bucket isolation.
  • The runtime controller receives a project member role. It does not receive user-administration or role-administration permission.
  • One shared controller user can serve many projects. Separate controller users also work because every project Secret contains a complete identity.
  • Compromise of a shared controller password affects all projects assigned to that user. Separate per-project Secrets reduce Kubernetes access scope but do not change the OpenStack identity scope.
  • The Composition owns per-Storage ProviderConfigs. The IAM bootstrap owns only OpenStack identities and role assignments. Operators apply the rendered project Secrets and the static EnvironmentConfig.
  • The bootstrap script does not remove users, role assignments, or Secrets. Operators must review dependent Storage resources before manual cleanup.
  • Removing a bucket requests deletion under Crossplane's default management policy. The Composition does not force deletion of a non-empty bucket.

docs.title: Implementation checks
docs.text: Test bootstrap idempotency, project binding, ownership checks, and credential recovery. Verify that the runtime user can create an EC2 credential for itself in the Secret's project but cannot administer users or roles. Test bucket creation, credential authentication, cross-project grants, None grants, and same-project access. Keep credentials out of Git, logs, and resource specs.

docs.title: Consumer Credential Strategy
docs.text:
Last reviewed: 2026-09-12

This document defines how bucket consumers receive and replace credentials. It is a living architecture strategy. An ADR records one accepted or proposed decision. This strategy connects those decisions and states the direction for future consumer authentication profiles.

Crossplane providers use separate credentials to create and delete cloud resources. Provider authentication differs by cloud and is outside the scope of this document. See the cloud IAM bootstrap guide. Provider credentials must never be published in a consumer Secret.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
Provider Storage must:

  • keep the public Storage API independent of the selected backend;
  • give common S3 clients a consistent connection contract;
  • support credential replacement without a new Secret reference;
  • limit every identity to its required resources; and
  • allow provider-native workload identity when the backend and consumer both support it.

docs.title: Current portable consumer contract
docs.text:
The Compositions create an S3 access-key pair for each credential generation. They publish the current pair in a Kubernetes Secret named after spec.principal, in the same namespace as the Storage resource.

spec.providerIdentity can set a shorter provider-native user name without changing the logical principal or consumer Secret name. Each backend applies its own naming convention to that identity.

Providers can also create generation-specific connection Secrets such as <principal>-20260911. Without rollover, the internal connection Secret is <principal>-credentials. These Secrets are provider-native. Consumers must use the stable <principal> Secret.

The required keys are:

  • AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
  • AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY

The optional connection keys are:

  • AWS_ENDPOINT_URL
  • AWS_REGION
  • AWS_S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE

A Composition must fail closed when a required key is absent. It must copy only the documented keys from a provider connection Secret. It must not copy an arbitrary provider result map.

This static access-key pair is the portable baseline for the backends and consumers that Provider Storage supports today. All current backend resource models can issue an access-key pair. Common S3 clients, including AWS SDKs and rclone, can use the same key names and endpoint settings. This contract does not depend on the cloud that hosts the Kubernetes cluster.

This baseline is not the only possible cloud-neutral design, and it is not the preferred credential type for every deployment. Static keys are long-lived secrets. They must be stored, distributed, rotated, and revoked. Provider-native workload identity avoids several of these risks when all parts of the request path support it.

docs.title: Rollover contract
docs.text:
ADR-002 defines static-key rollover. Provider Storage creates generation-specific credentials and keeps the configured number of generations active. It writes the current generation to the stable consumer Secret.

The overlap lets a consumer reload the stable Secret before the previous key is revoked. Rollover does not make a static key temporary. It also does not guarantee an exact rotation time. Rotation occurs during a successful Crossplane reconciliation after a period boundary.

The consumer must reload the Secret or restart before the overlap ends. Provider Storage does not force an application to reload its credential.

Operators must test both sides of rollover:

  1. The current and retained credentials can access only their allowed buckets.
  2. A generation outside maxToKeep is revoked.

docs.title: Other possibilities
docs.text:
Consumer credentials are used in different locations. Some clients run in the platform cluster. Others run in another cluster or outside the platform. The current portable contract therefore does not bind credentials to a client identity or execution location. It uses static access keys and scopes each identity as narrowly as the provider permits, typically to the declared buckets and grant modes. These credentials are still long-lived and transferable, so they remain a security risk.

A workload can fetch the current key pair through a credential helper or a protected HTTP endpoint instead of reading the consumer Secret directly. Clients that support the AWS credential chain can use a helper configured with credential_process or an HTTP endpoint (set AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI in the workload). A platform service could serve the current credentials from the consumer Secret through either interface. This does not require cloud STS or a custom STS service because the source remains the existing access-key pair. The helper or endpoint must authenticate callers and handle key rollover; the retrieved keys remain static cloud credentials. This is a possible workload integration, not a feature Provider Storage provides today.

When all consumers can be limited to workloads inside a supported cluster, a provider-specific profile can use workload identity federation. Where the cloud supports this pattern, its token service issues short-lived credentials for a Kubernetes service account. Examples are AWS IRSA or EKS Pod Identity with AWS STS, Microsoft Entra Workload ID on AKS, and GKE Workload Identity Federation. Each option depends on the cloud, cluster, and client credential chain. It also needs explicit selection and live trust, refresh, revocation, and teardown tests. These are possible future profiles, not current support promises.

docs.title: Security requirements
docs.text:
• Treat read access to a consumer Secret as access to its cloud permissions.
  • Enable Kubernetes Secret encryption at rest and use least-privilege RBAC.
  • Do not put consumer credentials in Git, logs, status fields, or command output.
  • Use an external secret manager when the deployment requires stronger controls than a Kubernetes Secret provides.
  • Scope consumer permissions to the declared buckets and grant modes.
  • Prefer temporary consumer credentials when a tested native profile is available.
  • Verify consumer revocation and access boundaries in the real cloud.

docs.title: Current state
docs.text: Area Current state Portable consumer credentials Static S3 access-key pairs in the stable consumer Secret. Consumer rollover Generation-based overlap through spec.credentialsRollover. Provider-native consumer identity Not implemented.

docs.title: Provider Storage backend differences
docs.text: The Storage API defines the same buckets, credentials, access requests, grants, and lifecycle rules for every backend. Each Composition maps that API to its provider's bucket and access resources. The table below compares the available implementations.

docs.title: Where access rules live
docs.text: Backend Bucket Identity and credential Access rule MinIO Bucket User with generated credentials Named Policy resources; the User lists their names. AWS S3 Bucket IAM User and AccessKey IAM Policy resources linked to the user by UserPolicyAttachment. OTC OBS Bucket IAM UserV3 and CredentialV3 One OBS BucketPolicy per bucket, with user IDs in Principal. OVHcloud Regional S3 ProjectStorage Project User and S3Credentials One consolidated S3Policy document per user, linked by its observed numeric user ID. CloudFerro Project-scoped OpenStack ContainerV1 One shared Keystone controller user with one EC2CredentialV3 per Storage generation The project owns access. An AWS S3 BucketPolicy uses the CloudFerro endpoint to share with another project's root ARN.

docs.title: MinIO
docs.text:
• Bucket: The Composition creates a MinIO Bucket for each configured bucket.
  • Identity and credential: It creates a User for each retained credential generation.
  • Access rule: It creates named Policy resources for owned buckets and grants. Each User lists the policy names that apply to that generation.

docs.title: AWS
docs.text:
• Bucket: The Composition creates an S3 Bucket for each configured bucket.
  • Identity and credential: It creates an IAM User and AccessKey for each retained credential generation.
  • Access rule: It creates IAM Policy resources for owned buckets and grants. A UserPolicyAttachment links each applicable policy to a user. The Composition does not create S3 bucket policies.

docs.title: OTC
docs.text:
• Bucket: The Composition creates an OBS Bucket. Consumers use its S3-compatible endpoint.
  • Identity and credential: It creates an IAM UserV3 and CredentialV3 for each retained credential generation.
  • Access rule: It creates one OBS BucketPolicy for each bucket named in the resource's buckets or grants. The policy contains the observed IDs of allowed users in Principal. The Composition must observe those IDs before it can build the policy.

docs.title: OVHcloud
docs.text:
• Bucket: The Composition creates a regional S3-compatible ProjectStorage bucket.
  • Owner: It creates a separate, stable project User without S3Credentials or an S3Policy. This user owns the buckets and keeps their owner ID unchanged when consumer credentials rotate or a credential user is replaced.
  • Identity and credential: It creates a project User and S3Credentials for each retained credential generation.
  • Access rule: It creates a separate S3Policy for each credential user. The policy allows or denies access to owned and requested buckets based on the owner's grants. See the OVHcloud access guide.

docs.title: CloudFerro
docs.text:
• Bucket: A composed OpenStack ProviderConfig scopes each ContainerV1 to the project in storages.pkg.internal/cloudferro-project-id. The required Composition selector uses provider: cloudferro.
  • Identity and credential: One controller user receives the configured member role in every managed project. The Composition creates retained EC2 credential generations for that user in the selected project.
  • Access rule: Users in one project can access its containers. For an active grant, the Composition reads the grantee Storage's project ID annotation and creates an AWS S3 BucketPolicy against the CloudFerro endpoint. The policy grants the grantee project's root ARN. It cannot isolate users in the owner project. Supporting resources retain the EC2 credential and AWS provider configuration until each bucket policy is deleted. See the bucket-sharing guide.

MinIO and OVHcloud both place consumer access on the user. MinIO users list multiple named policies. OVHcloud has one policy document per user, so the Composition combines all bucket rules into that document. AWS also uses user policies, but needs explicit attachment resources. OTC places the consumer grant rules on each bucket.

docs.title: From request to access
docs.text:
The requester records a target bucket in bucketAccessRequests. The bucket owner records its decision in bucketAccessGrants. These are fields on Storage resources; no backend creates a separate cloud request resource. The owner's grant selects ReadOnly, WriteOnly, ReadWrite, or None. The permission guide shows the resource fields and an example.

Backend Request pending, with no owner grant Owner grants access Owner sets None or removes the grant MinIO The request adds no policy name to the requester's User. The owner creates a named grant Policy; the requester lists that policy on each retained User. The requester stops listing the policy. With None, the owner's named policy has no allow statements. AWS The request creates no UserPolicyAttachment for the target bucket. The owner creates an IAM grant Policy; the requester attaches it to each retained IAM User. The requester has no attachment. With None, the owner's grant policy has no allow statements. OTC The request field does not change the generated policy. The owner's grant adds allow statements for the observed grantee ID to the bucket's BucketPolicy, even if the grantee did not record a request. The bucket policy has no allow statements for that grantee. None does not add an explicit deny. OVHcloud Each retained requester's S3Policy gets an explicit deny for the requested bucket. The policy replaces that deny with allow statements for the granted actions. While the request remains, the policy contains an explicit deny for that bucket. CloudFerro The request has no cloud-side effect. The owner adds allow statements for the grantee project's root ARN to the bucket policy. None or grant removal adds no cross-project allow. If no active grants remain, the bucket policy is removed. This does not restrict a user who is already in the owner's project.

For the owner-label requirement and the distinction between bucket visibility and access, see Discoverable Buckets.

OTC builds policies from the bucket owner's grants and observed grantee user IDs. It resolves each grantee principal through the matching discoverable peer Storage, then observes the provider-native user for that peer's current credential generation.

Removing a request also differs by backend. MinIO removes the grant policy name from the requester's users, and AWS removes the grant attachments. OTC does not use the request field, so removing it has no policy effect. OVHcloud removes the bucket-specific rule from the requester's user policy. OVHcloud then falls back to ACLs when no policy rule matches; removing a request alone does not prove that S3 access is denied. See the OVHcloud policy evaluation rules.

These descriptions are the resources the Compositions request. Cloud-side enforcement and revocation are asynchronous and need positive and negative S3 tests.

docs.title: Deletion behavior
docs.text: All bucket resources use the default Crossplane management policy. Removing a bucket from spec.buckets, or removing its Storage resource, requests bucket deletion. Deletion behavior is provider-specific. A provider can reject the request when it cannot empty the bucket or when its cloud identity lacks the required delete permission.

docs.title: Cloud IAM bootstrap
docs.text:
This guide uses these terms:

  • Bootstrap administrator: The person who runs iam.sh with an existing privileged login. Crossplane does not use this login.
  • Controller identity: The persistent machine identity that Crossplane uses through a ProviderConfig.
  • Consumer identity: An identity that Provider Storage creates for access to a bucket.

Review before deployment

Provider Storage needs permission to manage buckets, identities, policies, and access credentials. A cloud administrator must review the backend's iam.sh and policy files before running the bootstrap.

Run the IAM bootstrap before you render and apply its Kubernetes Secret manifest. No iam.sh accesses Kubernetes. For each backend that uses a static controller credential, apply writes a private local credential file. render-secrets reads only that file and prints the Secret manifest. Do not send this output to CI logs.

Provider installation and IAM bootstrap are independent. You can install the backend's providers and ProviderConfig resources before or after bootstrap. A managed-cloud Storage can become ready only when the rendered controller Secret is present and the provider configuration it needs is ready. For CloudFerro, the Composition creates a project-scoped OpenStack ProviderConfig during Storage reconciliation.

Backend Default controller credential file AWS ~/.config/provider-storage/aws-creds.json OTC ~/.config/provider-storage/otc-creds.json OVHcloud ~/.config/provider-storage/ovh-creds.json CloudFerro ~/.config/provider-storage/cloudferro-creds.json

Each backend-specific CROSSPLANE_<CLOUD>_CREDENTIALS_FILE variable can override its default.

The managed-cloud scripts use the same command model:

Command Behavior status Reads the cloud setup and local credential-file state. It does not change resources. apply Creates or updates the controller resources. It writes the local credential file when the selected mode uses one. verify Fails unless the required controller resources and credentials are ready. The exact live check depends on the backend. render-secrets Reads only the local credential file and prints Kubernetes Secret manifests. It does not call the cloud API or Kubernetes.

OTC also provides rotate-credential to replace its controller AK/SK. Run <cloud>/dependencies/iam.sh --help for required variables and backend-specific options.

Choose the bucket prefix during IAM bootstrap

Bucket names are user-facing. For AWS and OTC, the default prefixes are aws-<account-id> and otc-<domain-id>. Configure an override before bootstrap and use it for every Storage deployment. AWS enforces this prefix in IAM. The OTC prefix is only a naming rule. It does not limit the OBS Administrator permission.

docs.title: AWS identity model
docs.text:
The bootstrap administrator runs iam.sh with AWS administrator credentials. The script creates a controller runtime role and its inline policy.

The provider can use one of these base controller identities:

Mode Base controller identity assume-role An existing workload identity, such as IRSA or EKS Pod Identity static-user A dedicated IAM user with a static access key

The IAM user is a persistent controller credential user. It is not the bootstrap administrator. Its default path is /provider-storage/controller/crossplane.

In both modes, the base identity assumes the controller runtime role. The runtime role creates S3 buckets, consumer users, access keys, and policies.

docs.title: AWS permissions
docs.text:
The bootstrap administrator must be able to inspect and manage the IAM role, trust policy, inline policy, and tags. In static-user mode, it must also be able to manage the dedicated controller credential user and its access key. Review the templates in policies/ before apply.

The base controller identity can only call sts:AssumeRole for the controller runtime role. The runtime role can:

  • Manage users, access keys, and policies in the configured managed IAM paths.
  • Manage S3 buckets and objects with the configured bucket prefix.
  • Use the wider read and list actions that the provider needs.

The runtime policy denies changes to the controller credential user. Managed users and policies use /provider-storage/managed/. The default bucket prefix is aws-<account-id>.

docs.title: Run AWS bootstrap
docs.text: Follow the AWS dependency README for the required variables, both authentication modes, and the command sequence. Set the bucket prefix before apply; the runtime policy contains that prefix.

docs.title: Configure the AWS provider
docs.text: Both modes set the controller runtime role in assumeRoleChain. assume-role uses a workload credential source. static-user uses the generated aws-provider-creds Secret.

docs.title: Inspect AWS
docs.text: Use the same account, mode, prefix, names, paths, and credential-file value for all commands. status reports missing resources without changes. verify fails if the controller resources or credentials are not ready. See the integration test guide for the full deployment and S3 test.

docs.title: OTC identity model
docs.text:
The bootstrap administrator runs iam.sh with an existing OTC administrator login. The script creates one programmatic controller user, one controller group, and one permanent AK/SK. Crossplane uses that controller credential through its ProviderConfig.

The default user and group name is provider-storage-controller-crossplane. The IAM script does not adopt or delete resources that use older names. Consumer users start with provider-storage-managed-.

docs.title: OTC permissions
docs.text:
The bootstrap administrator must have Security Administrator at domain scope. The script re-scopes its OpenStack token to the target domain for the OTC IAM API.

The controller group receives:

  • Security Administrator at domain scope, so the controller can create consumer users and permanent credentials.
  • OBS Administrator for all existing and future projects, so the controller can manage OBS resources.

OTC cannot limit these system permissions to one bucket or bucket prefix. Use a dedicated domain for Provider Storage. An agency cannot replace the controller identity because OTC does not allow Security Administrator on an agency.

docs.title: Run OTC bootstrap
docs.text: Follow the OTC dependency README for the required variables and command sequence. The regional project ID selects the provider project. It is not the scope of the OBS Administrator assignment. IAM changes can take 10 to 15 minutes to take effect.

docs.title: Configure the OTC provider
docs.text: The ProviderConfig reads otc-provider-creds. After credential rotation, render and apply the Secret again.

docs.title: Inspect OTC
docs.text: status checks the group membership and both role assignments without changes. verify fails if the controller resources or credential are not ready. See the integration test guide for the full deployment test.

docs.title: OVHcloud identity model
docs.text:
The bootstrap administrator runs iam.sh with an existing OVHcloud administrator session. The script creates an OAuth2 controller service account and a project-scoped IAM policy. Crossplane uses the service account through its ProviderConfig.

The service account and IAM policy names start with provider-storage-controller-.

docs.title: OVHcloud permissions
docs.text:
The bootstrap administrator must be able to:

  • Read the target Public Cloud project.
  • Create an OAuth2 service account.
  • Create and update an IAM policy for that service account.

The controller policy is limited to the exact target publicCloudProject. It lets the controller manage the project resources that the Composition needs, including Object Storage users, roles, user policies, S3 credentials, and regional storage. Run status to see the exact action list before apply.

docs.title: Run OVHcloud bootstrap
docs.text: Follow the OVHcloud dependency README for the CLI preparation, required variables, and command sequence. The OVHcloud API region is separate from the Object Storage region.

docs.title: Configure the OVHcloud provider
docs.text: The ProviderConfig reads ovh-provider-creds. The EnvironmentConfig must contain the exact project ID and Object Storage settings.

docs.title: Inspect OVHcloud
docs.text: status reads the target project and matching IAM resources without changes. verify uses the controller credential to read the selected project and list its users. Share only redacted output. See the integration test guide for the provider Secret and bucket test.

docs.title: CloudFerro identity model
docs.text:
The bootstrap administrator runs iam.sh with an existing OpenStack login. The script creates one shared controller user without a default project. It assigns that user to each selected project. Crossplane uses a project-scoped configuration for this controller user.

The OpenStack project is the S3 access boundary. A user with S3 access in a project can access that project's containers. A bucket policy can share a bucket with another project's root ARN, but it cannot isolate users in the owner project.

docs.title: CloudFerro permissions
docs.text:
The bootstrap administrator must be able to:

  • List the projects that the configured name pattern selects.
  • Create one user in the project domain.
  • Assign the configured project role in every selected project.
  • Re-scope its token to the domain and projects when its initial login is project-scoped.

Re-scoping does not add permissions. The bootstrap administrator must already have the required domain and project permissions.

The controller user needs only the configured project role, which defaults to member. It must not have user-administration or role-administration permission. As a project member, it manages containers and creates an EC2/S3 credential for itself. The Composition also manages bucket policies.

docs.title: Run CloudFerro bootstrap
docs.text:
CloudFerro projects are billing resources and the access boundary for buckets. Create and activate all required projects in the CREODIAS billing portal before bootstrap.

Follow the CloudFerro dependency README for project preparation, required variables, and the command sequence. Limit the project pattern to the projects that the controller must manage. The script does not create projects or configure portal activation, wallets, or billing.

docs.title: Configure the CloudFerro provider
docs.text:
Each cloudferro-project-<project-id> Secret contains the controller identity and one project scope. The Composition creates a separate OpenStack ProviderConfig for each Storage.

Treat the project ID annotation as a privileged field. Restrict who can select a project and who can read its controller Secret.

docs.title: Inspect CloudFerro
docs.text: status checks the bootstrap login, project access, and selected projects without changes. verify checks project-scoped controller authentication and Object Storage access. The first live Composition run must also prove that the controller can create an EC2 credential for itself.

docs.title: Provider Storage installation guide
docs.text: Provider Storage lets platform operators offer S3-compatible storage through Crossplane. Install the dependencies and configuration package for each backend that you want to provide.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Choose a target namespace before deployment.

  • Apply Storage resources to the target namespace.
  • Provider Secrets and namespaced ProviderConfig resources must use the target namespace.
  • Provider Storage creates the consumer Secret in the same namespace as its Storage resource. The Secret name is the principal name.

EnvironmentConfig and Composition resources are cluster-scoped.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
You need:

  • a Kubernetes cluster;
  • kubectl access to the cluster;
  • Crossplane installed in the cluster.

For example:

helm repo add crossplane-stable https://charts.crossplane.io/stable
helm repo update
helm install crossplane crossplane-stable/crossplane \
  --namespace crossplane \
  --create-namespace \
  --set provider.defaultActivations={}

Provider Storage supplies a ManagedResourceActivationPolicy for each backend. It activates only the managed resource types that the backend uses.

docs.title: 1. Install backend dependencies
docs.text:
Choose a backend and follow its dependency guide. The guide contains the IAM bootstrap, credential Secret, provider configuration, and deployment steps for that backend.

Backend Dependency guide MinIO MinIO dependencies AWS AWS dependencies OTC OTC dependencies OVHcloud OVHcloud dependencies CloudFerro CloudFerro dependencies

The dependency manifests use the same order for every backend:

Manifest Scope Purpose 00-mrap.yaml Cluster Activates the managed resource types used by the backend. 01-deploymentRuntimeConfigs.yaml Cluster Configures provider and function deployments. 02-providers.yaml Cluster Installs the providers. 03-providerConfigs.yaml Target namespace Configures provider authentication. Apply it in every namespace that contains a Storage resource. 04-environmentConfigs.yaml Cluster Defines endpoint, region, and backend settings. functions.yaml Cluster Installs the Composition functions. rbac.yaml Cluster Grants the required provider-kubernetes access.

Edit all placeholders before you apply a manifest. Apply the numbered files in order, then apply functions.yaml and rbac.yaml.

Create the target namespace before you apply the namespaced ProviderConfigs. For example:

kubectl create namespace <storage-namespace>
kubectl apply --namespace <storage-namespace> \
  -f <backend>/dependencies/03-providerConfigs.yaml

docs.title: 2. Install the configuration package
docs.text:
After the backend dependencies are ready, create a Configuration manifest. Use the name and package for your backend:

Backend Name Package MinIO storage-minio ghcr.io/versioneer-tech/provider-storage/minio:0.4.0-rc.1 AWS storage-aws ghcr.io/versioneer-tech/provider-storage/aws:0.4.0-rc.1 OTC storage-otc ghcr.io/versioneer-tech/provider-storage/otc:0.4.0-rc.1 OVHcloud storage-ovh ghcr.io/versioneer-tech/provider-storage/ovh:0.4.0-rc.1 CloudFerro storage-cloudferro ghcr.io/versioneer-tech/provider-storage/cloudferro:0.4.0-rc.1

Use the selected values in this manifest:

apiVersion: pkg.crossplane.io/v1
kind: Configuration
metadata:
  name: <configuration-name>
spec:
  package: <package>

Replace <configuration-name> and <package> with values from the table. Replace 0.4.0-rc.1 with the package version that you want to install. Save the manifest as configuration.yaml, then apply it:

kubectl apply -f configuration.yaml

Wait until the configuration, providers, and functions are ready.

If the cluster has more than one Provider Storage Composition, each Storage resource must select its backend explicitly. A selector is not needed when only one compatible Composition is installed. See Select a backend.

docs.title: 3. Verify the installation
docs.text: Create a small Storage resource in the target namespace. Check that the resource becomes ready and that Provider Storage creates its consumer Secret. See Usage and concepts for examples and verification commands.

docs.title: Local integration tests
docs.text: Provider Storage uses an ephemeral Kind cluster for local integration tests. The cluster name is provider-storage-it. Every script uses the explicit kind-provider-storage-it context.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install Docker, Kind, kubectl, Helm, Crossplane CLI, and dyff. Run the full unit suite before integration:

tests/unit.bash

An agent must ask the operator before it creates the local test cluster. After approval, run:

tests/integration/create-cluster.bash

The command also creates the provider-storage-it namespace. The other scripts stop if this cluster is absent. They do not create it or use another current Kubernetes context.

docs.title: Test MinIO
docs.text:
MinIO needs no cloud IAM bootstrap:

tests/integration/run.bash minio

The integration command deploys Crossplane, MinIO, the required providers, and one MinIO Storage. It waits for the resource and its credential Secret, then verifies an object round trip and lifecycle cleanup.

docs.title: Test a cloud backend
docs.text:
Cloud tests use the same cluster. Before you run a cloud integration test:

  1. complete the backend procedure in the cloud IAM bootstrap guide;
  2. apply the provider credential Secret manifest printed by the IAM bootstrap; and
  3. run the provider and verification scripts for the selected backend.

The backend commands, credential formats, and multi-backend workflow are in tests/integration/README.md.

Run tests/integration/run.bash <backend> after the controller Secrets and required variables are ready. The command deploys the providers and test Storages, then runs the backend access checks.

List retained test resources by backend:

kubectl --context kind-provider-storage-it \
  get storages.pkg.internal \
  --namespace provider-storage-it \
  -L storages.pkg.internal/backend

The cluster is for a validation cycle. Remove it when the operator directs you to do so:

kind delete cluster --name provider-storage-it

docs.title: Provider Storage permission model
docs.text:
The permission model in provider-storage gives operators one access model across backends. Users work with four normalized permission levels instead of raw backend-specific IAM or policy actions. The Composition translates that model into the backend implementation.

  • ReadWrite: Full read and write access to bucket contents. Includes: ListBucket, GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject
  • ReadOnly: Read access. Includes: ListBucket, GetObject
  • WriteOnly: Write and delete access without object read access. Includes: ListBucket, PutObject, DeleteObject
  • None: Record that access is not granted by this resource. Backends differ in whether they remove an allow or write an explicit deny.

The backend comparison shows how each backend implements a pending, granted, or denied request and records current verification limits.

docs.title: Discoverable buckets
docs.text:
spec.buckets[].discoverable records whether a bucket should be shown to potential requesters. The Compositions do not use that field to decide access. Compositions that resolve requests from peer Storage resources require this label on the owner resource:

metadata:
  labels:
    storages.pkg.internal/discoverable: "true"

Once loaded, the Composition checks that the peer owns the named bucket and has a matching bucketAccessGrants entry for the requester. OTC uses observed grantee identities to build bucket policies; its current Composition does not inspect peer Storage resources for requests.

Example (owner Joe making his bucket discoverable):

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta1
kind: Storage
metadata:
  name: s-joe
  labels:
    storages.pkg.internal/discoverable: "true"
spec:
  principal: s-joe
  buckets:
    - bucketName: s-joe
      discoverable: true

docs.title: Request access
docs.text:
Other users can request access to a discoverable bucket by adding a bucketAccessRequests entry. Requests include the bucket name, a requestedAt timestamp, and optionally a free-text reason. The Storage API does not store a requested permission on the request itself; the effective permission is decided by the bucket owner's grant.

Example (Jeff requesting access to Joe’s bucket):

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta1
kind: Storage
metadata:
  name: s-jeff
spec:
  principal: s-jeff
  buckets:
    - bucketName: s-jeff
  bucketAccessRequests:
    - bucketName: s-joe
      reason: Need access for collaboration
      requestedAt: "2025-09-29T10:10:00Z"

Until Joe explicitly grants access, Jeff’s request remains pending.

docs.title: Grant or deny access
docs.text:
The bucket owner decides whether to grant or deny a request. This is captured with a bucketAccessGrants entry, which specifies:

  • The bucket name
  • The grantee
  • The granted permission (ReadWrite, ReadOnly, WriteOnly, or None)
  • The timestamp when the grant or denial was recorded (grantedAt)

Example (Joe granting Jeff ReadOnly access to s-joe):

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta1
kind: Storage
metadata:
  name: s-joe
  labels:
    storages.pkg.internal/discoverable: "true"
spec:
  principal: s-joe
  buckets:
    - bucketName: s-joe
      discoverable: true
  bucketAccessGrants:
    - bucketName: s-joe
      grantee: s-jeff
      permission: ReadOnly
      grantedAt: "2025-09-29T10:15:00Z"

If Joe wanted to record a denial, he would set permission: None in the grant. Whether this produces an explicit cloud policy deny depends on the backend.

docs.title: Permission lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Bucket owner marks bucket discoverable.
  2. Requester adds a bucketAccessRequests entry with the target bucket, timestamp, and optional reason.
  3. Owner responds with a bucketAccessGrants entry.
  4. If permission is one of ReadWrite, ReadOnly, or WriteOnly, access is granted.
  5. If permission is None, the resource records a denial; the generated policy behavior differs by backend.
  6. Callers supply requestedAt and grantedAt timestamps for traceability.

This keeps the workflow visible: requests, reasons, grants, and denials remain in the Storage resources for operators to inspect.

For a complete two-principal example, see Joe and Jeff.

docs.title: Provider Storage usage and concepts
docs.text:
This section explains how to use Provider Storage after installation. Users request buckets and access through a Storage resource. The platform controls the backend, policies, credentials, lifecycle rules, and credential rotation.

Buckets, credentials, access requests, access grants, and lifecycle rules use one API. The backend implementation differs, but the user-facing model stays the same.

See the backend comparison for provider-specific identity, policy, and verification limits.

docs.title: Select a backend
docs.text:
If the cluster has only one compatible Provider Storage Composition, Crossplane can select it without a Composition selector. If the cluster has more than one backend Composition, set an explicit selector on each Storage resource. Valid provider values are aws, cloudferro, minio, otc, and ovh.

spec:
  crossplane:
    compositionSelector:
      matchLabels:
        provider: minio

All backends use the storage EnvironmentConfig by default. Set the storages.pkg.internal/environment annotation or label to select a different EnvironmentConfig. The multi-backend examples select storage-<backend>.

CloudFerro also requires the storages.pkg.internal/cloudferro-project-id annotation and an explicit provider: cloudferro Composition selector. See the CloudFerro dependency guide.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
For every Storage resource, access credentials are created for spec.principal and stored in a Kubernetes Secret in the same namespace. The Secret is named after the principal and uses the same S3 keys on every supported backend.

Set spec.providerIdentity only when the provider-native user needs a different short name. This does not change the consumer Secret name.

Applications and other platform building blocks can consume this Secret directly. For example, a Datalab can use it to mount object-storage access into a workspace.

Credentials can be rolled over on a schedule. A configurable number of older credentials can stay valid during rotation, which avoids disruptions for running workloads.

docs.title: Buckets
docs.text:
A Storage resource defines one or more buckets for a principal. Each bucket is created on the selected backend.

Buckets can be marked discoverable so clients can show them to potential requesters. The field does not enforce access; the owner's grant and the backend policy do. See Discoverable Buckets for the owner-label requirement in request workflows.

docs.title: Lifecycle rules
docs.text:
Buckets can define lifecycle rules under spec.buckets[].lifecycleRules. The Storage API defines one lifecycle rule model across backends. Rules target either the whole bucket (*) or a prefix such as tmp/*, then either delete matching objects or report them without changing data.

Delete removes matching objects when the time condition is met. Notify logs matching objects when the time condition is met and does not change objects.

Supported minAge suffixes are s seconds, m minutes, h hours, d days, and w weeks. Rules may alternatively use at with an RFC3339 timestamp for a fixed UTC cutoff.

docs.title: Access requests and grants
docs.text: A principal records a request for another bucket in spec.bucketAccessRequests. The bucket owner records the decision in spec.bucketAccessGrants. The request does not contain a permission. The owner selects ReadOnly, ReadWrite, WriteOnly, or None in the grant. See the permission model for discovery requirements and backend differences.

docs.title: Joe’s Storage resource
docs.text:
# Joe creates one discoverable bucket s-joe, requests access to Jeff's bucket,
# and grants Jeff ReadWrite access to s-joe.
# Credentials are static and do not rotate automatically.
apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta1
kind: Storage
metadata:
  name: s-joe
  labels:
    storages.pkg.internal/discoverable: "true"
spec:
  principal: s-joe
  buckets:
    - bucketName: s-joe
      discoverable: true
  bucketAccessRequests:
    - bucketName: s-jeff-shared
      reason: Need access
      requestedAt: "2025-09-29T10:00:00Z"
  bucketAccessGrants:
    - bucketName: s-joe
      grantee: s-jeff
      permission: ReadWrite
      grantedAt: "2025-09-29T10:05:00Z"

docs.title: Jeff’s Storage resource
docs.text:
# Jeff creates two buckets, requests access to Joe's bucket,
# grants Joe ReadOnly access to one of his own buckets, cleans
# tmp/ under the shared bucket after twelve hours, and notifies
# on week-old scratch/ data.
# Credentials are automatically rolled over every week,
# keeping the current plus the previous credential active.
apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta1
kind: Storage
metadata:
  name: s-jeff
  labels:
    storages.pkg.internal/discoverable: "true"
spec:
  principal: s-jeff
  credentialsRollover:
    interval: weekly
    maxToKeep: 2
  buckets:
    - bucketName: s-jeff
    - bucketName: s-jeff-shared
      discoverable: true
      lifecycleRules:
        - target: tmp/*
          mode: Delete
          minAge: 12h
        - target: scratch/*
          mode: Notify
          minAge: 1w
  bucketAccessRequests:
    - bucketName: s-joe
      reason: Need access
      requestedAt: "2025-09-29T10:10:00Z"
  bucketAccessGrants:
    - bucketName: s-jeff-shared
      grantee: s-joe
      permission: ReadOnly
      grantedAt: "2025-09-29T10:15:00Z"

In this example:

  • Joe owns s-joe and Jeff owns s-jeff and s-jeff-shared.
  • Joe requests access to s-jeff-shared, Jeff requests access to s-joe.
  • Joe grants Jeff ReadWrite access to s-joe.
  • Jeff grants Joe ReadOnly access to s-jeff-shared.
  • Jeff cleans tmp/ in s-jeff-shared and reports week-old scratch/ objects.

docs.title: Example: Jane requesting access from John
docs.text:
# Jane has no buckets but requests access to John's bucket and explains
# in the reason that she wants WriteOnly access.
# Note: This request only becomes effective once John grants it.
# Credentials are automatically rolled over every quarter,
# keeping the current plus 4 previous credentials active.
apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta1
kind: Storage
metadata:
  name: s-jane
spec:
  principal: s-jane
  credentialsRollover:
    interval: quarterly
    maxToKeep: 5
  buckets: []
  bucketAccessRequests:
    - bucketName: s-john
      reason: Need WriteOnly access
      requestedAt: "2025-09-29T10:20:00Z"

A Storage resource can contain only access requests and create no buckets.

docs.title: Example: John responding to Jane
docs.text:
# John owns s-john. He grants Jane ReadWrite access to his bucket even though
# Jane's request reason asked for WriteOnly access.
# His request to s-jane cannot resolve until that bucket exists.
# Credentials are automatically rolled over every day.
apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta1
kind: Storage
metadata:
  name: s-john
  labels:
    storages.pkg.internal/discoverable: "true"
spec:
  principal: s-john
  credentialsRollover:
    interval: daily
  buckets:
    - bucketName: s-john
      discoverable: true
  bucketAccessRequests:
    - bucketName: s-joe
      reason: Need access
      requestedAt: "2025-09-29T10:25:00Z"
    - bucketName: s-jeff
      reason: Need access
      requestedAt: "2025-09-29T10:26:00Z"
    - bucketName: s-jane
      reason: Need access
      requestedAt: "2025-09-29T10:27:00Z"
  bucketAccessGrants:
    - bucketName: s-john
      grantee: s-jane
      permission: ReadWrite
      grantedAt: "2025-09-29T10:28:00Z"

In this scenario:

  • Jane requests access to s-john and records WriteOnly intent in the request reason.
  • John grants ReadWrite access, so Jane receives broader access than she requested.
  • The system reconciles and attaches the effective permission.

docs.title: Verify provisioning
docs.text: After you apply a Storage resource, check that provisioning completed.

docs.title: Check resource status
docs.text:
List all storages in your namespace, for example workspace:

kubectl get storages -n workspace

You should see READY=True once reconciliation is complete. Example:

NAME          SYNCED   READY   COMPOSITION        AGE
s-jane        True     True    storage-minio      2m
s-joe         True     True    storage-minio      2m
s-jeff        True     True    storage-minio      2m
s-john        True     True    storage-minio      2m

To see more detail, describe the composite:

kubectl describe storage s-joe -n workspace

Look for conditions like Ready=True and check any event messages.

docs.title: Find the consumer Secret
docs.text:
Each Storage resource produces a Secret in the same namespace named after spec.principal. For example, the resource s-joe with principal s-joe creates a Secret named s-joe. Do not use internal Secrets such as s-joe-credentials or s-joe-20260911. Providers create them with provider-native key names.

List Secrets in the namespace:

kubectl get secrets -n workspace

Inspect the Secret:

kubectl describe secret s-joe -n workspace

View raw YAML (keys are base64-encoded):

kubectl get secret s-joe -n workspace -o yaml

Decode credentials locally. For example, use these commands for AWS-style keys:

kubectl get secret s-joe -n workspace -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}' | base64 -d; echo
kubectl get secret s-joe -n workspace -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}' | base64 -d; echo

All providers expose only AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and the configured connection keys in the normalized Secret. The connection keys are AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, AWS_REGION, and AWS_S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE.

You can now use these credentials with any S3-compatible tool. For example:

aws s3 ls s3://s-joe

All buckets, access requests, and grants in this resource are owned and managed under this principal. true bucketAccessGrants []object Grants issued by this principal to other principals.
